analysis.one_liner: Gives federal regulators power to test, label, and restrict the sale of tobacco products, especially to minors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 1992 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it never received a hearing or a vote; it had no cosponsors and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The Tobacco Health and Safety Act of 1992 would have created a new chapter in federal food and drug law for tobacco products. It would have barred sales to anyone under 18, banned free samples and coupon discounts, required manufacturers to disclose every additive and submit each brand for government testing of tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide, required a prominent 'Federal Law Prohibits Sale to Minors' statement on packaging, and changed the Surgeon General's warning to say that smoking is addictive [S2] [S3]. The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, particularly children: the bill aimed to keep tobacco out of the hands of minors, expose what chemicals are in each brand, and give consumers stronger, more honest warnings about addiction. The bill's own findings note that 60 percent of new smokers start before age 14 and that smoking is the leading preventable cause of death [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell or distribute tobacco products to anyone under 18, and requires states to enforce the age limit, with backup federal authority if state enforcement falls short [S2] [S3].
Requires manufacturers to disclose every additive and lets the government test and publicly disclose tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels for each brand before it can be sold [S2] [S3].
Bans free samples and coupon or discount promotions for tobacco products [S2] [S3].

Replaces the existing cigarette warning with a direct statement that 'Smoking is Addictive. Once you start you may not be able to stop,' and lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services strengthen warning labels without weakening the health message [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, importers, and packagers, who would bear the costs of testing, additive disclosure, and new labeling, and lose free-sample and coupon marketing channels. Tobacco retailers that rely on promotional sales would also lose those sales [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban tobacco; it regulates it. Someone would still be able to buy cigarettes legally as an adult, and the bill states explicitly that it does not prohibit manufacturers from providing truthful additional information [S3]. A good-faith objection is that regulation here focuses on information and youth access rather than reducing adult smoking directly.

The bill requires manufacturers to submit additive lists and brand testing to the Secretary before products can lawfully be sold, which imposes compliance costs on the industry; critics could argue these costs would be passed to consumers through prices, though the bill's findings put the public cost of smoking at over $60 billion a year in lost productivity and health care [S3].

Enforcement depends heavily on state-level implementation for the youth-access provisions, with federal requirements on the form, manner, or location of sales available only if state enforcement is found insufficient [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health stakes are large: the bill's findings describe tobacco as the single most preventable cause of death and disability in the United States, with 60 percent of new smokers starting before age 14 [S3]. The costs fall mainly on tobacco manufacturers and on promotional marketing, a concentrated industry interest. The bill is an information-and-access bill rather than a ban, so its immediate effects on consumers are modest, but its youth-access and testing provisions address the leading preventable cause of death.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 1992 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the Tobacco Health and Safety Act of 1992 in the Senate on February 27, 1992 [S1] [S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill never moved past committee; there is no recorded hearing, markup, or floor action, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and the promotional marketing around their products were better off: they faced no new testing, disclosure, labeling, or youth-access requirements, and tobacco remained among the least regulated consumer products, as the bill's own findings put it [S3].

for.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract any cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the remainder of the 102nd Congress

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Cigarette, cigar, and smokeless tobacco companies
against.what_they_did: The bill would have subjected their products to federal testing, additive disclosure, stricter labeling, a ban on free samples and coupons, and a hard age floor on sales; the industry historically opposed federal tobacco regulation and promoted tobacco to adults as an adult practice, per the bill's own findings

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan breakdown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to disclose all additives, submit every brand for government testing of tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide, carry a prominent 'Federal Law Prohibits Sale to Minors' label and an addiction warning, and give up free samples and coupon promotions. Because the bill died, none of these requirements took effect and tobacco remained among the least regulated consumer products [S2] [S3].

Retailers and distributors would have been barred from selling to anyone under 18 and from distributing free samples or honoring coupons and discounts for tobacco products. The bill died, so those restrictions never applied [S2] [S3].
